subsubtopic: ALLEGED ERRONEOUS INFORMATION IN REPLY TO QUESTION ON THE ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I have given the Chair a copy of the grievance that I bring to the attention of the House. I have also contacted the office of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) to indicate to him that I wanted to rise today on a question of privilege.
Needless to say, if you determine that I have a prima facie case of privilege I am willing to move the necessary motion to bring this matter to the appropriate parliamentary committee.
It is a long custom in the House that Members of Parliament are to provide other members factual information and only the truth. As a matter of fact, I am sure you will remind Hon. Members that to assume that any Member of the House ever states anything but the truth would be, in itself, a breach of the Standing Orders of the House. Of course, all Members of Parliament are deemed to be honourable members and therefore one expects to hear the truth in the House and nothing else.
I want to bring to your attention the fact that I placed Question No. 2 on the Order Paper in June last year. Question No. 2 was replied to on October 1 by the Minister of Public Works. I will read the question and answer and make them available to the House. The question I posed to the Government was:
1. Did the Government employ the services of Colvin Designs Ltd. and/or Giovanni Mowinkle, interior designer during the period September 4, 1984 to June 30, 1986, to supply furnishings, improvements, interior decorating or advice on same for the Prime Minister's residence at 24 Sussex Drive in Ottawa or the Harrington Lake residence and, if so, by residence, what was the cost of each contract?
The second question was also on the Order Paper. It was the following:
Was all of the work paid for from Government funds and, if not, who paid such costs and what was the amount involved in each case?
The reply was: "No" to the first part of the question and: "Not applicable" to the second part.
It has come to my attention, as reported by a Toronto newspaper, The Globe and Mail, that in fact the Government of Canada through the National Capital Commission paid an invoice or invoices amounting to $38,414.60 for furnishings and services to 24 Sussex Drive and that these funds had been paid to either Giovanni Mowinkle, Colvin Designs or both. This appears to be in contradiction to the first part of the question that I asked. With respect to the second part of my question the Minister indicated that it was not applicable.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that even if all the funds had been paid by someone else the fact remains that Mr. Mowinkle appears to have performed work and to have been compensated for that work.
April 27, 1987

I submit that because we are talking about a property that belongs to the Crown, government property, the response of the Minister should have at least described the fact that, indeed, Mr. Mowinkle and/or his firm did in fact perform work at 24 Sussex Drive as well as at the Elarrington Lake residence.
For Your Efonour's consideration I wish to offer a decision made by the Speaker in 1978. At that time the Hon. Member for Northumberland-Durham raised a question of privilege in the House of Commons concerning the fact that the then Solicitor General had written to him and provided to him information which later proved to be erroneous. On December 6, 1978, the Speaker indicated, as reported at page 1857 of Hansard: "I, therefore, find a prima facie case of contempt against the House of Commons".
The point I am making is that if it was a contempt against the House of Commons to provide a Member of Parliament with erroneous information, then surely to provide the House itself with erroneous information through a written reply to a question on the Order Paper would, as far as I am concerned, also be a prima facie case of privilege.
I must say that if this is a legitimate mistake, and if the Minister is willing to indicate that it is, then I am prepared to discontinue pursuit of the matter. However, in the absence of such a reply from the Minister I will let my request stand before you, Mr. Speaker, to have it considered a prima facie case of privilege and to be referred to the appropriate parliamentary committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Stewart Mclnnes (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to my hon. friend for giving me appropriate notice and for allowing me to postpone my response to this time rather than having to respond this morning.
I want to affirm that Colvin Designs was hired to perform services at 24 Sussex Drive. An invoice was subsequently submitted for services rendered. The National Capital Commission reviewed the work and determined that it was appropriate for the NCC in its role as custodian of official residences to pay for the expenditures invoiced. Accordingly, payment in the amount of $38,414.60 was made on July 10, 1986, a date outside of the September, 1984 to June 30, 1986 timeframe specified in the Hon. Member's question.
In preparing the original reply only accounts paid as of June 30, 1986, the date specified by the Hon. Member, were examined. There was no attempt whatsoever to mislead the House. I am pleased to have this first opportunity to clarify this matter for the House and to set the record straight.

Did the Government employ the services of Colvin Designs Ltd. and/or Giovanni Mowinkle, interior designer during the period September 4, 1984 to June 30, 1986, to supply furnishings, improvements, interior decorating or advice on same for the Prime Minister's residence at 24 Sussex Drive in Ottawa or the Harrington Lake residence and, if so, by residence, what was the cost of each contract?

speechtext:
I want to thank the Hon. Minister for being frank. As well, the House is indebted to the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) for accepting the explanation, and accepting it in good grace.
I am sure the Hon. Minister will carry the message back to those who are charged with the responsibility to answer written questions, with the request that, as the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) has indicated, they read the questions carefully before providing an answer.

Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable emotion that I rise in the House today to speak to this important motion which deals with a proposal to reinstate capital punishment in Canada. Mr. Speaker, depending on the position the House will take following this debate, men and women will live or die. All members present must realize that when the time comes to vote on the motion, if they nod their heads in favour, they will be killing themselves, as it were.
I have made no mystery about my position on this issue. I am firmly opposed to reinstating capital punishment, and I want to explain to Hon. Members and to the people of Canada my reasons for taking this stand. Mr. Speaker, in Canada as in so many other countries, capital punishment has been the subject of countless debates in the past years.
In fact, at the beginning of April in Great Britain British parliamentarians, notwithstanding the polls, had the courage to vote for the eighteenth time against reinstatement of capital punishment. Since the Canadian judiciary system is quite similar to the English system I would suggest that at the very least this result should cause everyone of us to give serious consideration to the position to take here.
April 27, 1987

Mr. Speaker, the debate has a particular character because it contains legal, philosophical, religious, moral and scientific aspects. Personally, as a practicing Catholic, the question I am asking myself is much more directly related to the sense I give to human life than to the sentence which should be imposed for a foul crime.
Morally speaking, I feel that taking a life is harmful to both the state and the citizen. The state must give the example by acknowledging the sacred character of human life in every instance.
A 1977 International Conference on the Abolition of Capital Punishment ended with the adoption of the Stockholm Declaration which stated that the duty of the state is to protect the life of every citizen. It strongly urged all countries to abolish the death penalty. More recently a number of groups were established to speak out against the reinstatement of capital punishment. In a recent message, the Conference of Churches, the Conference of Catholic Bishops wrote this, and I quote:
The death penalty is acceptable only in a society which is not sufficiently well
organized to defend itself by other means. This is not the case of Canada, a
country which has made enough progress to find other ways than the death
penalty to protect itself.
I have also received many letters from constituents and people from across Canada, who oppose the reinstatement of the ultimate penalty. Criminology experts also made their opposition known and I would like to quote among others from Andre Normandeau who wrote in La Presse on Thursday, March 12: I personally oppose the death penalty for both personal and professional reasons. On the personal level, it is my view that if the democratic State proposes its citizens two great values, liberty and due regard for life, it should set an example by refusing to kill legally a human being, even where the latter's murder is despicable. Under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, all citizens are equal and there can be no exception to due regard for life.
In an interview with Maclean's magazine, the famous criminologist Edward Greenspan also flatly opposed it. So did the Canadian Association of Social Workers, the Canada Jewish Congress and many others. The widow of Rev. Martin Luther King, Mrs. Coretta Scott King, during a recent visit to Ottawa, went on record against the reinstatement of the death penalty in Canada. She felt that Canada would take a step backward by reinstating capital punishment.
According to recent surveys on that important matter, it would seem that a majority of the Canadian people favour the reinstatement of that ultimate penalty.
As far as I am concerned, I circulated a questionnaire in my constituency and the majority of respondents favoured the death penalty. But the result was different on the question of deterrence.
Mr. Speaker, should we base on chancy surveys our decision on such a basic question? My sincere answer is: No.
Capital Punishment
Hear, hear.

Indeed, if we asked Canadians whether they favoured a significant tax reduction, I am convinced that more than 90 per cent of the people would favour such a move. As elected representatives, should we then ignore sound management principles to meet the desires of the electorate? Once again, my answer is no. And on such a vital question, I feel that each and everyone of us must make an enlightened choice on the basis of the information available to him or her, and above all, must follow the call of his or her conscience.
This penalty is absolutely, fundamentally degrading on the human level, because it proclaims the uselessness of the guilty person's life. It also precludes the achievement of one of the three main goals of punishment, rehabilitation. Those who favour non-capital solutions defend the respect of all human life and urge society to rehabilitate and reform the offender. I am one of those.
Philosophers like Plato, Hobbes, Rousseau held that virtue can be taught and punishment must aim at correcting the offender's wrong inclinations. The goal must be to reform criminals and to deter them from relapsing to crime and also to maintain order.
In many cases, people who resort to violence have had an unhappy childhood which did not allow them to become responsible citizens.
Yet, it is the responsibility of any civilized society to impose on delinquents punishments which can contribute to their rehabilitation.
Eleven years ago, the abolitionists, as they are sometimes called, managed to eliminate capital punishment from our national statutes and mores. As Pierre Tremblay wrote in an editorial in the April 2 issue of the newspaper Le Devoir, "In 1976, a small majority of six votes in the Commons extirpated this relict of barbarism from our penal code, just as one has a bad tooth removed, with pain and apprehension."
Some uncertainty remained then. Were we not opening the door to second offenses? We are now forced to admit that we did not. Over the past ten years, the number of crimes which theoretically should carry the death penalty has not increased. We were right in 1976 when we felt that the supreme penalty had no real value as a deterrent. I am convinced that its reinstatement in 1987 would not prove different.
As a matter of fact, the deterring effect which is the major argument of all those who are in favour of capital punishment must be examined most carefully. If all punishment has a deterring effect, capital punishment has value only if it has this effect, no matter how limited. The question then is whether capital punishment has a more deterring effect than life imprisonment.

April 27, 1987
Capital Punishment
The theory of deterrence is based on the notion that the commission of a crime depends on the chances the guilty party feels he has of getting away with it. As legislators, we must consider deterrence as a means of preventing crime and also provide for more severe punishment in order to increase the fear of punishment in the potential criminal and reduce the frequency of crimes.
We must therefore determine whether the state of our knowledge warrants this approach and, therefore, the reinstatement of capital punishment.
Criminology studies have clearly shown that there is no significant correlation between the death penalty and the murder rate. In Canada, since capital punishment was abolished in 1976, the rate has remained stable at 2.5 murders per 100,000 inhabitants. While capital punishment was enforced between 1970 and 1974, the average was 2.3 murders for 100,000 inhabitants.
Mr. Speaker, we have no choice but to admit that there has been no wave of violence since 1976. The classic example of the United States is also interesting. Let us compare two American states somewhat similar socially and economically, on the one hand Michigan, which includes the City of Detroit, which abolished capital punishment in 1847, and on the other hand Illinois, which includes the City of Chicago, which has maintained capital punishment. We find that over a period of nearly 140 years, the difference is no more than 5 per cent between the two states for the murder rates in general and those of police officers and prison guards in particular. Incidentally, the difference sometimes works out to the advantage of Michigan and sometimes to that of Illinois, so the statistics certainly do not argue in favour of a return to the death penalty.
At the University of California, David Phillips got the debate going again in 1980 with a study in which he qualified the death penalty as an immediate and temporary deterrent. He writes: "We get the impression that a potential murderer delays his crime for a few weeks after an execution is publicized in the media." According to Phillips, we must not expect this to have a comprehensive and permanent effect. He cites the example of drivers on a highway who slow down to look at the victims of a serious accident and are slow to pick up speed again, although ultimately, they often exceed the speed at which they were driving before they stopped.
According to Phillips, the same applies to homicide. During the two weeks following a publicized execution, the homicide rate goes down. However, within five or six weeks after the execution, this drop is cancelled by an increase in the number of homicides. After six weeks, the rate goes back to normal. At the end of the year, the total number of victims is the same as if no execution had taken place.
Mr. Speaker, would the answer be to execute someone every two weeks?
Phillips does not dare make such a recommendation and notes with regret that his field of reference, 22 executions
which took place in London between 1858 and 1921, does not include any instance where executions took place in quick succession. I therefore conclude that we have very little evidence of the deterrent effect and that in view of the very serious nature of the act involved, a civilized State should look for other deterrents.
The most valid reason to oppose capital punishment may be the possibility that an innocent might be killed. Last Friday in Montreal, an inmate called Pepin was released from prison. He had been accused of armed robbery, and had been in jail for eight months when the real culprit came forward. This man had been saying from the beginning that he was innocent. However, he was wrongly accused of robbery. No system whatsoever can guarantee infallability in passing judgment.
There have been cases in the past where people were put to death by mistake, and in spite of all the safeguards of our present-day system, there is still a possibility that this might happen. The Leader of the Opposition mentioned this morning that in 1982, Donald Marshall, who had been accused of murder and sentenced to death, was released after spending 11 years in a New Brunswick penitentiary. As for Wilbert Coffin, a prospector who was hanged in 1956, there are still questions after so many years as to whether he was really guilty.
On December 8, 1983, the British Minister of Justice released from prison Mervin John Russel, aged 39, who had been declared guilty of murdering a 20-year old female student. In 1977, when the case was reviewed, it was shown that the tuft of hair found in the hand of the victim did not come from his scalp. On August 23, 1977, the Governor of the State of Massachusetts, Michael Dikakis, declared innocent and rehabilitated Bartolomeo Vanzetti and Nicholas Sacco who had been executed exactly 50 years earlier, on August 23, 1927, after being declared guilty of murder.
Mr. Speaker, can we afford to take such risks? Would it mean that people would be better protected? Quite frankly, I do not believe they would, and I even think it would be the opposite. It has been shown over the years that executions appealed to the minds of morbid individuals, and could cause imbalanced people to take criminal action. The punishment itself may therefore cause more violent crimes, and provide some people with an inspiration to act violently.
Examples abound. Police departments for instance frequently refuse to publicize suicides or attempted suicides as it has been shown that such revelations lead to an appalling concatenation of other suicides. The news of a suicide prompt suicidal attitudes in other people. If that is true in such instances, there is a clear and easily applicable law: violence will lead to more violence.
In a society like ours, we must coordinate our efforts to put in place more effective policies of crime prevention in the legal, medical, social and educational fields. Our role as a just society is to emphasize prevention and to take all the means to that end. As long as this is not done it is useless to propose something as cruel as the death penalty. This is opposing
April 27, 1987

violence to violence without really dealing with the source of the problem. Crime is a social problem and we have to go to the heart of it, rather than choose a superfical solution that does not solve anything.
Mr. Speaker, we do not have the right to decide arbitrarily on the fate of our brothers, sisters, children and grandchildren. Our society has always attached much value to and shown a great respect for life and it must eradicate the causes or factors of crime. It must also, for humanitarian reasons, try to improve the correctional system so that the sentence imposed to criminals contributes to their rehabilitation and their social integration.
For all these reasons, and others 1 did not have time to develop, I will vote against restoration of capital punishment in Canada.
The reinstatement of capital punishment in Canada not only could make us lose any credibility in the area of rights and freedoms, but it could also be a signal for reinstating capital punishment in other countries. How could Canada in the future boast of defending rights and freedoms in international organizations, and more specifically the United Nations Human Rights Commission, if we gave such a clear indication that we do not honour our commitments and signature. Our credibility could easily be questioned.
Can we as a society take such a responsibility? 1 will conclude, Mr. Speaker, by stating that, personally, if the death penalty were to be reinstated in Canada, I would find unacceptable such a violation of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which prohibits any cruel and unusual treatment and punishment. Reverting to the ultimate sentence would negate what we have supposedly become, a more civilized, vanguard nation, a land of freedom, a model around the world.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Duplessis) for her most eloquent, passionate and moral speech which reflects the opinion of a great many Canadian men and women. I would like to ask her how the feelings of Quebec men and women may differ from those of their fellow Canadians, and since most Quebecers continue to maintain contacts with the Catholic Church, what are the views expressed in that province by Catholic bishops and priests and what influence they can have, if any, on this debate. Does she believe, as I do, that here, in the Parliament of Canada, it is our duty to listen to the advice of religious men and women, the pastors of the various Churches, the philosophers and all those who are concerned with moral issues? I fully appreciate the moral position she has just expressed. I share it myself. However, perhaps in order to help some of our colleagues here in the House, I would like to know whether she believes that in a Canadian society which adheres to Judeo-Christian values, even though it increasingly includes the teachings of the other major religions in the world as it becomes more multicultural, we, in Parliament, should listen to the advice of our religious leaders and what advice is being given by Catholic priests in Quebec on this issue.
Capital Punishment

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend opposite for having appreciated the speech I made during the present debate. I shall be pleased to answer his question.
To begin with, I should like to say to my hon. friend that the views of Quebecers on capital punishment are no other than those of other Canadians. If he has carefully considered opinion polls published for some time in various newspapers, he has probably noticed that Quebecers were exactly of the same opinion as Canadians throughout the country. However I am glad to note a difference among Members of Parliament from Quebec. Most of them are against the reinstatement of capital punishment. They have publicly said so.
Hear, hear!

It is true that the Council of Churches, our clergy and parish priests have told us that if we are really practising Christians and believers, we have to be against capital punishment. However, before such statements were made, I had already taken my decision. It only confirmed what I believed in that respect.
Morally speaking, there is something that we should not forget and that is also valid for our colleagues and other individuals throughout the country as well as all other religious denominations in Canada. The reinstatement of capital punishment means that one does not believe in the rehabilitation of the human being who could come to regret his wrongdoings, try to grow better and finally serve the Canadian people. It amounts to losing faith in mankind.
Personally, I do not think that a human being can become rotten. A rotten apple cannot improve. It will only get worse and become uneatable. However, the human being is different. When a human being receives good advice, is being taken good care of and loved, feels it has his or her rightful place in life, there is always a hope that he or she will turn over a new leaf and become better.
So I brought here a small clipping where various solutions are indicated by the Council of Churches. There is also something I would like to bring to your attention, and if I am not mistaken, this morning, during the debate, I think your leader referred to this about the Council of Churches, when he asked how many people know that more than a third of all murders are committed within the family, in the home, after some quarrel? This applies to the majority of crimes in Canada.
This means that there may be something wrong in society. I referred to that earlier. We know that misery and poverty can lead to crime. We are told that maybe we should look more closely at that, this is where we should be providing support. As Members of Parliament we should work twice, a hundred times as hard at improving well-being in society, whether helping children or looking for better regional distribution across Canada. Members from every part of the country and every Party in this House will have to learn how to live with a decision we have taken in order to help and raise the standard

April 27, 1987
Capital Punishment
of living in one part of the country, in order to stamp out misery in areas of this country. Members from everywhere will have to learn to respect that.
We cannot claim to be Christians, and indeed Mrs. Luther King said she cannot imagine Christians who support killing others. This is my answer concerning the ethical side, the recommendations made by the bishops.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to commend the Hon. Member for Louis-Hebert (Mrs. Duplessis) for her excellent speech on capital punishment.

I would like to ask a question of the Hon. Member with regard to the process upon which we are embarking today. The Government has decided to initiate a debate here in the House that no doubt will take several months to conclude. This particular discussion centres around a resolution, not legislation, but a resolution to endorse capital punishment in principle. We know that this particular portion of the so-called debate on capital punishment may take several months, if not longer. Following a determination of this resolution in the House, a committee will be struck which will travel across the country for three months and then report back to the House. The Government has been criticized for the process of prolonging the discussion of this very moral and important issue.
Has the Hon. Member taken the opportunity to voice her concerns to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and to her colleagues in Cabinet to indicate to them that it is wrong for the Government to stretch out this debate over such a long period of time? The Hon. Member knows I agree wholeheartedly with her position on the issue, but I think it is wrong for the Government to embark on the process it has.
[DOT]	(1550)
1 would ask the Hon. Member if she would undertake to try to use her resources, her good offices and her powers of persuasion to convince members of her own caucus to accept and adopt the position she has taken. The Hon. Member will recognize that the overwhelming majority of her own caucus supports the resolution in principle.

In reply to my friend the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata), who was talking about the process, Mr. Speaker, may I say that there might be no process if ever a majority of members decided to vote against the reinstatement of capital punishment. When my Government decided to proceed this way, it was first of all, as you know full well, to fulfill a promise made during the last election campaign. One should fulfill one's promises. As a matter of fact, you are constantly reminding us that we have made promises in other areas.
On the other hand, you should not overlook the way it was done. It was done to respect democracy. It is a process which is quite democratic, which meets the requirements of my colleagues who are in favour of reinstating capital punishment. We made a commitment, and we are living up to it.
Contrary to my hon. friend, I feel that my Government is doing the right thing in holding this debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry, but the period for questions and comments is over. Debate. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon we are called upon to debate a very important issue in the House of Commons. It is one that goes beyond partisanship of any kind and one that is very difficult for all Members of the House.
I would like to take a moment to discuss the manner in which this topic was brought to the attention of the House of Commons. A government Minister tabled in the House a motion and then immediately dissociated himself from the motion he had presented. The motion, of course, calls upon the House of Commons to give its favour in principle to a resolution calling for the reinstatement of capital punishment.
The Government claims that it can dissociate itself from the motion it has itself put because this will be a free vote. I would argue that that is incorrect. There is no historic precedent for proceeding that way in a Parliament. If some Hon. Members wish to indicate that there is a parallel because of a free vote that had taken place in the past, I would argue that there was a substantial difference between the two. In the last free vote, the Government introduced a motion and unanimously supported it within Cabinet yet the Government tolerated dissension within its own caucus. That is far different from having a cabinet Minister present a motion to the House and then immediately saying that he was not necessarily for it or against it or that the Government was not necessarily for it or against it. I would submit that this unprecedented move on the part of the Government is indeed what I would consider to be morally inappropriate when dealing with such a topic.
Cowardly.

Some would even say, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) has just said, that it is cowardly.
The debate started today with the Parliamentary Secretary to the government House Leader as the lead-off speaker. Instead of speaking to the issue of capital punishment which his own Government had introduced, he spent most of his time congratulating himself and the Government for perceived past accomplishments and he warned the House not to take too much time because the Government wanted to deal with the pornography Bill, patent legislation and other issues in the
April 27, 1987

future. Therefore, he said, Members could take the time they wished but of course he reminded us of all those other important things which Parliament must do in the future. I wonder, if those issues were so important, why they were not dealt with before bringing this motion to the attention of the House of Commons.
The Government hangs its hat on saying that this was a campaign promise and it had to deliver. Where is the precedent for such action? Relatively no other campaign promises have been delivered to date so what is the special initiative that is necessary in this particular case?

Mr. Speaker, this debate is unfortunate. It is unfortunate because it shows just how desperate a political Party can be: this Conservative Government will introduce just about any legislation to improve its political credibility. I can tell you that when a political Party stoops so low to improve its image, we have a major moral problem. Mr. Speaker, I urge you and all our colleagues in the House to consider the way the Government went about presenting this motion to the House, and specially its timing.

Nevertheless, today we are dealing with an important debate. It is important because it deals with life itself. I have deeply held views on the topic and so do others. Some have views which differ considerably from mine but they believe in them with as much conviction as I believe in my own.
It is unfortunate that in some cases the debate has been trivialized by individuals either stating that those who did not want to reinstate capital punishment were in favour of criminals or that those who are in favour of the reinstatement of capital punishment are of equally devious minds. I do not believe that either is the case. Nevertheless, it is unfortunate that such statements are being made as one which was attributed to a Member of the House by Maclean's magazine, which indicated that an Hon. Member referred to capital punishment by saying: "Hang 'em high and hang 'em often". Remarks like those are very unfortunate and remarks made in the opposite direction would be equally wrong in my view.

Mr. Speaker, since 1867, 710 people were executed in Canada. The last two were put to death in 1962. They were Arthur Lucas, aged 54 and Robert Turpin, aged 29. Since then, Canada has effectively abolished the death penalty. At first, at the turn of the century, capital punishment was imposed for murder, treason, rape and gradually, as our society became more and more civilized, we first eliminated public hanging, then capital punishment for other offences and finally, as I said earlier, in 1962, Mr. Diefenbaker abolished the death penalty de facto since he and his successors chose not to reinstate it.
Capital Punishment
Finally, in 1973, the Government put temporarily an end to the death penalty through legislation and in 1976, it was abolished for good.
There are reasons which some people give for the reinstatement of capital punishment. Let me outline some of them and say why I do not think they are appropriate. First we have the argument of, shall we call it retribution? In other words, someone who has killed does not deserve to live. While at first blush that argument may have a certain attraction to some people, I must say that it certainly has no place, in my view, in a civilized society which claims, as we do, to have a good and sound system of justice. We do not rob the robbers. We do not beat the beaters. We do not burn down the arsonist's house. We do not rape the rapist. It of course is equally true that we do not murder the murderers.
The theory of deterrence has also been used by some as a reason for capital punishment. That is no more effective or reasonable an idea than that of retribution. I say that for this reason. In 1975 there were 701 homicides in Canada according to statistics I have obtained. In 1985 it was 686. In 1986 it was 561. Considering that this country's population is increasing it holds true, in my opinion, that the absence of capital punishment certainly has not resulted in an increase in murders. The murder rate per 100,000 people in Canada was 2.7 in 1976 and is now about 2.5. We know that in the U.S. the murder rate is
8.49	per hundred thousand. That is over three times what it is in Canada. However, even if we look at it in a regional sense, because capital punishment is a state responsibility in the U.S. and not federal as it is here, the state of Minnesota, an abolitionist state, has a murder rate of 1.7. Gun-toting Texas has a murder rate of 14.2. That leads me to believe that violence breeds more violence and we should not for that reason reinstate capital punishment.
Of those countries in the western world Belgium has the lowest murder rate. Before someone says that Belgium still has capital punishment, I want to remind the House that it has not been used since 1945. Belgium's murder rate is 1.03. That should lead us to some conclusions when we compare it to the
8.49	rate in the U.S. Of course, the U.S. has executed some 38 people since 1977.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about potential errors. As the House will know, Mr. Wilbert Coffin was executed in 1956 for a murder of which he was convicted at the time; Mr. Raymond Cook, in 1960, was also put to death in Alberta.
To date, Mr. Speaker, a large number of Canadians, including some parliamentarians, have grave doubts about the execution of those two people, wondering whether they were really guilty.

April 27, 1987
Capital Punishment
I would also like to mention three other miscarriages of justice involving murder cases, although they did not lead to a death sentence being carried out. We had Kenneth Roberts in 1977, Derek Cole in 1978, and finally, Donald Marshall who was released in 1982 after his case was reviewed, 11 years after he was sent to prison. He was innocent. And though some people point out that Mr. Marshall was not convicted of premeditated murder and would therefore not have received the death penalty, I want to take this opportunity to inform the House that the same principle applies, namely that if a mistake was made in the case of Donald Marshall, how can we guarantee that mistakes were not made in other cases?
Senator Howard Metzinbaum of the United States tabled in the U.S. Congress a list of 48 people who were found guilty of murder and subsequently declared innocent, while Michael Radelet, an American researcher, puts this figure at over 100 since the turn of the century. If for no other reason, and I have just given a number of examples, I think the reason I have just touched upon here should be sufficient for a civilized country like Canada to want to terminate this debate on the death penalty immediately and not pursue the matter further.
Mr. Speaker, I may add that the United States is the only Western country that still practices capital punishment. Belgium still has it on the books, and Ireland as well, but practically speaking, since 1945 and 1954, respectively, it is no longer applied in those countries. Mr. Speaker, Canada must not be allowed to regress. The Conference of Catholic Bishops issued a communique which was distributed to members on February 24, and it reads as follows:
Today, ten years after the abolition of capital punishment, we still hold the same conviction: A society that respects the sacred and spiritual character of human life and which has human rights as its first priority, is slowly and perhaps not always spectacularly, but at any rate surely, on the road to social progress for itself while contributing to the development of mankind. This conviction, confirmed by the message of John Paul II when he visited this country, is based on the message of the Gospel in which mankind is redeemed of its sins by Jesus Christ and thus reconciled with God.
Innocent, but convicted as a criminal and sentenced to death, Jesus himself showed us the way of total forgiveness: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do."

I now want to go back to the topic I raised a few moments ago concerning retribution and its so-called merits. I received a letter in my office on March 5, 1987, and it reads as follows: "I would like you to consider my views on capital punishment in light of the motion currently being debated. Our 11-year old daughter, Alison, was abducted and murdered last July. Prior to Alison's death I had always been opposed to capital punishment, this conviction being based upon the very deep Christian belief that it is wrong to kill another human being no matter what the circumstances. Alison's murderer has given me a very strong personal and agonizing experience of the horror of violence and killing. It has more than ever convinced me that we as a society cannot ever and must not ever condone killing, whether by state or individual, in any shape or form. Throughout this debate much attention has been focused on
the victim's rights. While I agree that often the safety, security and suffering of present and future victims is not always given due consideration, I do not believe that anyone suffering can in any way be alleviated by the deliberate killing of other human beings. I do not want to be part of a society that brings up future generations with the belief that killing can be legitimized under certain circumstances. Let the message be clear and unconditional; human life is sacred, killing is always wrong. Please consider my deep-felt views and vote no to the return of the death penalty".
That letter is signed by Mrs. Lesley C. Parrott, the mother of Alison Parrott who, unfortunately, as we all know, was an 11-year old child who was murdered.
In conclusion, it is my opinion that the time of the House should be spent on many other issues. We should be spending a lot of time on the issue of illiteracy as well as a lot of time trying to find employment for our constituents who are out of work.
We are talking about the murder rate, which is 2.5 per 100,000, but are not even mentioning the fact that the suicide rate is 13.8 per 100,000 and that a large percentage of that relates to young people. We are not taking time to discuss the many other problems which our society is facing right now.
Although I know that 70 per cent of Canadians in general, and probably a similar number of my constituents, are in favour of reinstating capital punishment, it is important to note that only 5 per cent consider the issue to be important. I indicated my opinion to the voters in the last election. They knew where I stood before they elected me to the House of Commons. I indicated clearly to them that I had no intention of participating in a process which would reinstate capital punishment.
In conclusion I want to remind you of the words of Edmund Burke spoken 213 years ago. He said:
Your representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment; and he
betrays, instead of serving you, if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
Those are my views, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that the House will defeat the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I notice that the Hon. Member who has just spoken referred, as did his Leader, to the statements of Edmund Burke. I have also noticed that a lot of editorial writers, with surprising selectivity, constantly urged Members of Parliament to ignore or defy the clear opinion of the public by citing this portion of Burke's speech to the electors of Bristol in 1774. He said at that time:
Your representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment; and he
betrays, instead of serving you, if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
Those who do not confine their reading exclusively to editorials will be aware of the fact that after the dissolution of Parliament in 1780 Mr. Burke found that the electors of Bristol were so violently opposed to his attitude that he wisely decided not to stand for renomination.

Does he have anything to say to elderly people who are afraid to walk on the streets-and I know some of my constituents who feel that way because they are afraid of being attacked. There are a lot of trigger-happy individuals around these days. Think about the many corner grocery store owners who have been shot dead by thieves, by second offenders who do not hesitate because they know they will be paroled after seven years even after having been sentenced to life imprisonment. Mr. Speaker, what solutions does the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) have to offer Canadians who want capital punishment applied in this country, something which the previous Liberal Government has never done?

Mr. Speaker, let me tell you in plain language that it takes nerve, it takes a lot of nerve for an Hon. Member on the Government side to stand on his feet in this House and ask the Opposition if it has an alternative for better government. That takes a lot of nerve coming from the Government side, Mr. Speaker, I must say. All the more so when a government Member rises to ask us for an alternative to the death penalty. Is there an alternative between life and death? Can one be so ridiculous as to put such a question to the House? I must recall that if there is a problem with parole,
Capital Punishment
then an appropriate solution must be found. In any other area as well, if there is a problem, then a solution must be found. You do not execute prisoners because no alternative has been found, even if one's Government has come to office with the largest majority in Canadian history. What a sorry excuse to give this House, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member as well as her Government should be ashamed to raise such issues.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to know if my colleague is aware of studies which indicate that juries do not impose the death penalty, that they are reluctant to do so? Is he aware that such studies exist? Is he willing to make any comment?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague from Winnipeg for a very relevant question. He is quite right in raising this matter, because a poll has indeed been taken among people who had served as jurors previously. Very clear results were obtained from that survey in which former jurors were asked: Madam or Sir, had you had to reach a decision knowing the penalty would be death, would you have found the accused guilty in the very case you decided in the past? To a large extent, Mr. Speaker, those Canadians who sat on juries said no, because there was still some doubt in their minds that kept them from sentencing-not sentencing because it is the judge not them who sentences-but they would not have made any move which might have resulted in sentencing somebody to death. So that is very interesting, and we could conclude that indeed the restoration of the death penalty could have a totally reverse effect in the sense that a greater number of those guilty of murder could be released because the jury would be somewhat reluctant to find them guilty. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) has drawn our attention to a very interesting fact.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) and others in favour of capital punishment argue that they must respond to the wishes of their constituents. They believe that due to the fact that 70 to 75 per cent of Canadians favour the return of capital punishment they must, as a result of some duty, respond by voting for capital punishment notwithstanding what their own personal beliefs may be. I want to say to the Hon. Member for Peterborough and others-

Will the Hon. Member agree that it is wrong for a moral, civilized nation to have retribution or revenge as the basis for its criminal justice system? Would he agree that it is basically the law of the jungle that dictates that type of basis for a justice system?

Very briefly, Mr. Speaker, perhaps Gandhi put it best when he said something to the effect that if justice was still administered on the basis of an eye for an eye, we would have a society that would be totally blinded by now.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I will begin my remarks today by commenting on what has been discussed by the member who just spoke and others in his Party. 1 want to respond to the comment that more murderers would be loose on the streets because juries would be more reluctant to convict them. My source in arguing that point is a letter that I received from Norman S. Douglas, Q.C., Crown Attorney, District of Algoma. He said:
In the two dozen murder cases that I have prosecuted, I have not encountered any sympathetic juries for first degree murderers.
However, even if it is conceded that juries would be more cautious in convicting if the result was capital punishment, second degree murder is always an included offence.
In short, if a jury felt too squeamish about convicting on first degree they would convict of second degree instead. Thus, the killer would receive a sentence of life imprisonment. It is simply misleading to say that if a person is not convicted of first degree murder then he walks out of the courtroom.
That is the kind of misleading information that turns what could be a sensible, logical debate into the resurrection of arguments that cannot be substantiated and are only the whims and fancies of abolitionists who care little at all about a true justice system that provides the kinds of penalties that convicted murderers deserve for that act of planned, deliberate, premeditated murder.
Let me add that we are not looking to murder everyone who commits, or execute everyone-
You said murder. You are going to murder them.
I will deal with murder in a minute.
The state will murder. That is what you said.
We are not looking to execute the some 700 innocent people who are murdered by people who are guilty of planned, deliberate, premeditated murder.
Murder. That is what he said.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Let me take some of my 20 minutes to give what I believe is the best explanation of why we are at this point today in the House of Commons concerning the subject of capital punishment.
For the second time in the last few years, the United Kingdom turned down a motion for a return to capital punishment. I am not prepared to say that I could have supported that motion either because those who have done more research than what is printed in the abolitionist newspapers will know that that motion would not have been supported in this House of Commons either because it called for a return to capital punishment for planned, deliberate, premeditated murders, providing the jurors found the murders to be evil. We are not talking about evil murders, but planned and deliberate murders that do not have to be considered evil. I will not get into a debate on whether acts of treason and terrorism are evil or whether we are talking about someone who is against the Government because it is doing something that it should not be doing.
We are talking about four, five or possibly six types of planned, deliberate murder for which there is a clear consensus in the country that there should be capital punishment. It remains to be seen whether the Opposition will vote according to their conscience. I suspect that the New Democratic Party has no conscience and does not have the luxury of voting according to their conscience.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I hesitate to interrupt the Hon. Member in mid-rant, but I want to call to Your Honour's attention that it is quite improper to ascribe motives to any Member of the House with respect to their participation, particularly in a debate as serious as this.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Mr. Speaker, it is accepted that the New Democratic Party cannot vote according to conscience because they have taken a party position based on policy that has been adopted by a convention of the New Democratic Party.

The Liberals also have a problem with the issue of conscience. There are Liberal Members of Parliament who are former Cabinet Ministers who supported capital punishment at the time of abolition. In a debate with myself on Canada-AM, a frontbencher in the Liberal Official Opposition stated that he supports capital punishment. He said on Canada-AM that he voted against capital punishment in 1976. When asked what he would do with respect to the Conservative motion in support in principle of capital punishment, he said that he would vote against it. I question the ability of some members of the Liberal Party to vote according to their conscience.
Let me deal with four or five points that have been made by other members. I do not believe any religion in Canada has an exclusivity on who is Christian and who is not Christian. I can list for the record ministers, clergy, of church denominations of all types who have written me as the heads of their churches in complete support of a return to capital punishment. They include the Oxford Baptist Church, Woodstock, Ontario; the Fundamental Baptist Mission; a letter from a former padre in the United Church; a letter from Pastor Jake Giesbrecht of the Ferndale Bible Church in Peterborough, Ontario; a letter from Reverend Hutson, T. How many bishops have you got, and name them? Name the bishops who support your view.

-on religious grounds. I sit in the House of Commons and I stand here today and I will debate with any member opposite who says to me that someone says that someone else is not a Christian because they support capital punishment. Who are they judging-whoever "they" might be? I do not propose to judge any member of the Opposition as being Christian or anti-Christian. I think members opposite are on pretty thin ice when religious leaders of the country judge other religious groups, organizations, churches and theologians as anti-Christian because they support capital punishment because of the teachings in the Old Testament and because of the teachings in the New Testament. Members opposite say that nowhere in the New Testament does Jesus Christ endorse capital punishment. I challenge Hon. Members opposite that nowhere in the New Testament does Jesus Christ say that the state does not have the right to take another person's life.
Let he who is without sin throw the first stone.

Having said that, if Hon. Members opposite support capital punishment because of teachings in the Old
Capital Punishment
Testament, then I challenge them to show me why the person who supports capital punishment because of teachings in the Old Testament is any less Christian than someone who supports or is against capital punishment because of teachings in the New Testament.
Let us deal with the idea that was brought forward here today in debate by the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition when he talked about capital punishment being barbaric or being uncivilized. This is the "capital punishment is murder" argument all over again.
What the abolitionists assert here is: "Uncivilized barbarians kill; all killing is uncivilized and barbaric; therefore judicially ordered executions are uncivilized and barbaric."
That quote is from Les Bewley, a retired Vancouver criminal court judge and columnist for the magazine Canadian Lawyer. He also stated:
This contraption may sell, but only to those who have forgotten, or never knew, that civilization depends upon the rule of law-that code which prohibits antisocial, harmful and murderous acts under pain of punishment by a court of justice and denies to the individual the right to enforce his own justice, vengeance or revenge. To assert that execution is merely barbarism or revenge is to deny the very meaning and process of civilization and to murder reason itself.
The other argument is that capital punishment is murder. I have heard that not only on this side of the House but from members opposite as well.
That's what you said a minute ago.

Let me tell the Hon. Member what Mr. Bewley said on the topic. He said;
"Murder is killing; execution is killing; therefore execution is murder." That's like: "Confining a person is unlawful; judges confine people, therefore judges are breaking the law"-The murderer is prosecutor, judge and jury, all without lawful authority. Only such killing can be called murder.
In absolute contrast, society provides an accused murderer with all the rights and safeguards he has denied to his victim. If then, after proof of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, society sentences him to death, that is not murder; it is as far from unlawful killing as it is possible to get. To call this murder is to speak a lot of nonsense.
Let me tell Hon. Members that that quote is also from Les Bewley and is contained in Canadian Lawyer. The article appeared in The Globe and Mail on March 19, 1987.
I also want to read Hon. Members one little article which I think can say it best. I worked over the weekend trying to figure out where we got where we are, why we are not satisfied-
Because of people like you is why.
-that the vote in 1976-when I say "we" I mean the Canadian people. You might not represent the Canadian people.
I certainly do.

Add to that the rise of vigilanteism here in Canada, which I do not support, and I have a difficult job trying to explain why people in Canada will give from their pockets their hard-earned cash to store-owners who try to defend property and life against criminals. What causes that?

I predict two things today-and these are not matters that I came to lightly. I predict, first, that Parliament will be required to amend the Criminal Code, bringing in stiffer penalties, including capital punishment in certain circumstances, as a result of this debate; and secondly, I predict that, if the Senate refuses to pass the Criminal Code amendments as passed by the elected representatives of the people, supported by the majority of the Canadian people, the Government will embark on a program of major Senate reform, urged by the Canadian people to do just that.
In our parliamentary system of Government, the Government has the responsibility to represent constituents. When it comes to an issue of conscience, I realize the difficulties involved. I was raised as an abolitionist, the son of a United Church minister. I know the positions taken by abolitionists, and I respect those positions. What bothers me is that the abolitionists tend, very often, to personalize the debate, going so far as to call those who do not agree with them antiChristian.
I have yet to hear a retentionist in Canada call another church leader anti-Christian because of that leader's support for abolition. Why do the abolitionists persist in this low-level debate, personalizing positions rather than discussing conscience?
A question raised earlier today was: Is there any deterrence effect in having capital punishment on the books?
No.

I can give you the names of 14 people who would be alive today, innocent people who would be alive today, had that first-time murderer been executed.
Those are 14 crimes that would have been prevented. For those who bring up the half-way house case in Ottawa, the Sweeney case-I am not dealing with Sweeney because it is now under appeal-I remind those individuals that the father of the victim in that case is a determined and devout abolitionist, and I respect that position. But the mother of that girl who was raped and murdered in the half-way house now supports capital punishment. That is something that should be mentioned. The mother of that girl went on national television to voice her support for capital punishment.
Just this past month, we have learned of a series of chainsaw murders in Montreal. We had 17 pieces found of one victim of a chain-saw murder.
Capital Punishment
I am sick to death of reading in our newspapers and hearing on radio and television about the suffering of someone who was executed. What about the 11 children in British Columbia who were raped and murdered and then buried along the highway? What about the Montreal victim whose body was cut up into 17 pieces? What about the young girl who was raped and murdered in the half-way house? What about Eli Guay? What about the six convicted murderers who, having been paroled, murdered again? What about the judges? What about the jurors? What about these judicial reviews?
If an individual, having gone through all of the steps in our criminal justice system, is found guilty of first-degree murder, that individual should be executed. We do not have one known case of wrongful execution in Canada since Confederation. No such case has ever been produced to me. Yet, I can produce dozens of names of innocent people who have been murdered as a result of the judicial review process. The same judiciary who say we should not execute because we may execute the wrong person have caused, indirectly, the murder of dozens of innocent people because of their judgment as to who should and who should not be paroled.
Is it more ethical to be bigoted when it comes to judicial review than when it comes to murder? I support capital punishment for planned, deliberate, premeditated murder; murder arising from a hijacking or hostage-taking incident; contract killers, hired guns; and for serial killers. As well, I support capital punishment for the killing of police officers and law enforcement agents, and prison guards.
Until this debate ends, whenever it ends, I will be fighting for the return of capital punishment for those six offences. I am prepared to produce, name for name, those in support versus those opposed. I think the people need to be heard, and the Government needs to respond. This Government, the Progressive Conservative Government, has shown some responsibility in this respect. This will be the first true free vote on this matter since Confederation. All of the other "free votes" had solid blocks of cabinet Ministers voting for abolition. We have one individual sitting in this House who was a member of the Cabinet at the time of the last "free vote" on capital punishment, and he at that time, notwithstanding that he was a retentionist, voted for abolition as part of the cabinet block of votes; and I can give you the names of two others who were in a similar circumstance in 1976. Had those three individuals voted for retention in 1976, we would still have capital punishment on the books today. All we needed were three more votes, and we had three supporters of capital punishment who voted for abolition. These three individuals polled their constituents and came out and said they supported capital punishment, and in fact spoke in support of it. Yet, as part of the cabinet block of votes, they voted against it.
The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) has now offered the Canadian people the opportunity to have their elected representatives cast a free vote on this question. The elected representatives of this country are responsible to their

conscience, their constituents, and their Party. I am proud of the Progressive Conservative Party for allowing this question to be debated; I am proud of the Party for allowing members of Cabinet to vote as they see fit. I respect the abolitionists, and I expect the same in return. This is a debate which should not be personalized.

Has the Hon. Member for Peterborough now had a chance, after hearing the words of the Parliamentary Secretary, to
reflect upon what he said earlier? Is it still his view that if the House should not adopt the resolution by June 30, it would be a sign that his Prime Minister and his Government are in fact weak and vacillating on the issue? Is that still his position?

Mr. Speaker, let me make it abundantly clear that it was the statement of the Deputy Prime Minister's office, as quoted in the paper at the time we delayed the debate from March until April, that it was still the intent of the Government to deal with this issue before the end of June and bring back within 90 days a report to Parliament on the proposed amendments-when capital punishment would be applied and which type of execution method would be used.
I stand firm on what I said. I feel we have set our own timetable. It must be obvious to anyone watching the debate, or anyone who has followed it with any amount of interest over the past number of months, that the New Democratic Party has only one objective, that is, to filibuster, delay, and not make it possible to put the vote. We have offered every opportunity to both the NDP and the Official Opposition to cause the debate to end as quickly as possible. We have offered to stay late at night, sit weekends, or limit speeches to 15 minutes, and they turned down every opportunity to limit the debate and get on with the vote.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Hon. Member. I wish the Hon. Member would accord as much right to differ with him on this issue to members who oppose capital punishment as those of us who oppose capital punishment accord to him, the right to his belief in capital punishment.
With the exception of the United States, every democratic country of which I know has refused capital punishment, such as Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, France, Belgium, Holland, Spain, Australia, and New Zealand. I will also mention Great Britain and Israel, two countries which are constantly facing the real threat of actual assassinations of people in their countries. All those countries have refused to have capital punishment as part of their judicial system.
Why is it that the Hon. Member, instead of thinking that we should follow their example, wants us to follow the example of communist countries and countries with military dictatorships, all of which have capital punishment?

Mr. Speaker, I think we should point out first that the United Kingdom still has capital punishment for acts of treason in its Criminal Code. I think we should also point out that Canada still has capital punishment in our military law. The Hon. Member should know this. He should not even have asked the question because one of his members has a Private Members' Bill to abolish it from our code in military law.
I think he should also know about the situation in the United States where they have returned to capital punishment. If we add up all the states which have capital punishment and take the average per year over the last five years, we see that those
April 27, 1987

states have had decreases in their homicide rates at a much faster clip than the other states. The good news is that in the United States, where they returned to executions in 1977, they have had an annual decrease in not only the number of homicides from 23,000 per year down to 17,800 last year, for which complete figures are available, but they have decreased 23 per cent in their homicide rates. We do not enjoy that luxury, except in the occasional year when we have a drop, and then it goes back up.
We had the largest number of homicides in Canada in 1985. There were 700 and some homicides in Canada. That is nothing to be proud of. In the United States it is going down at the rate of 23 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) has listed a series of crimes which he believes warrant capital punishment. Does he not think that instead of having this debate on the opportunity of reinstating capital punishment, it would be better to examine the possibility of implementing a full employment policy so that we might reduce the number of starving people, and of youths resorting to prostitution, or getting into drugs and then having to shoplift and go on to hold-ups? Does he really think capital punishment is a deterrent for criminals, and does he not remember that in Chicago, at the time of A1 Capone and his gang, it was not the death penalty that put an end to the massacres, but the Income Tax Act that sent those people to jail? And as a last question to the Hon. Member, since he is in favour of reinstating capital punishment, would he be ready to act as the hangman to execute those he wants put to death?

Mr. Speaker, I think I should take the time to point out that during the time the Liberals were in office violence in Canada or violent crimes rose in 1962 from 41,000, according to a Statistics Canada report, to 179,000 when they lost office in 1984.
What is he telling me about the reason for the violent crime increase being as astronomical as that? What about attempted murders during their time in office? They rose from 83 in 1962, as reported by Statistics Canada, to 922 in one year, in 1984. What did they do about reform in our justice system? What did they do about our parole system and mandatory supervision?
1 suggest that the Hon. Member should start looking in the mirror. The reason we are in a mess today is because of their inadequacy in dealing with criminals and major capital offences, and now first degree murder. The first degree murder rate in Canada has gone up from 202 in 1980 to 300 and some in 1985.
What about 1986?

It dropped in 1986, but those were only temporary figures. What about the 329 people, homicides, all
Capital Punishment
of whom went down in the Air India air crash? Not one of them was reported by Statistics Canada.
If we add that 329 figure to the homicide rate, we would have the highest homicide rate in Canadian history. The Indian investigation has already determined that the crash was caused from an explosion in the luggage compartment, which makes Canada fully responsible. It is our homicide rate. There were deaths, and they do not even appear in the Statistics Canada homicide figures for 1985 or 1986. However, they will appear and we will catch up.
